newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - US to glean little from steady rates.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US to glean little from steady rates.

text.p: Bond markets are increasingly confident the U.S. Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates this week but that does not mean Treasuries will charge ahead against other government debt, analysts said on Monday.
Uncertainty about inflation is likely to dog the U.S. market for some time to come and this will continue to push open the yield gap between T-notes and German Bunds, analysts said.
"I think there's more room on the downside on a surprise hike than there is room for a rally on no change," said Tom Rayner, economist at SGST in London.
"I think the market will be quite surprised if we get a hike this week," Rayner said.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meets on Tuesday and Wednesday. A recent Reuters poll showed 25 out 26 economists expected rates to be held steady, with the federal funds rate at 5.25 percent and the discount rate at 5.00 percent.
Tim Fox, economist at Standard Chartered said he saw a rate move coming but not this week.

"It's tight, but I suspect they can just hold off this time around," he said. "Obviously we've seen strong growth in the U.S., but we've seen that before, and it doesn't automatically translate into higher interest rates, particularly as inflation remains pretty subdued."
Rayner said he expected the Fed to make its move at the next FOMC meeting on March 25.
Nevertheless, analysts said steady rates would not save Treasuries from underperformance against Bunds in the short-term.
The T-note/Bund 10-year gap is currently at 93 basis points.
Rayner saw it widening out to 100 over the month, possibly reaching 110.
"We're still quite bearish on the U.S.," he said. "We think the trend is still for that spread to widen. One hundred basis points would seem like an obvious target."
Rayner said SGST was looking for seven percent on the 30-year U.S. bond. It was trading at 6.81 percent at 1421 GMT.
"The market's getting a little bit optimistic, rallying so strongly on last week's data," he said. "Seven percent still looks a target, fundamentally and technically."

U.S. data out last week on the whole reassured markets inflationary pressures had not yet come through but also showed continued economic strength, analysts said. Bunds would benefit from data showing an economy still sputtering.
"The underlying strength is still there in the U.S.," said Rayner. "But if you look at Germany, almost the opposite is true."
He said German unemployment figures due Thursday could reach an all-time high and fuel speculation Germany may struggle to meet the deficit criteria for entry to monetary union (EMU).

"They may well have to cut rates at some later stage this year," he said. "The weakness of the mark has helped them a bit...but I still think there's room for rate cuts in Germany and almost the opposite situation in the States."

But Williams de Broe economist David Smith said he thought a rate cut in Germany was unlikely in the near future since proposals are underway for major tax reforms which could involve cutting top rates of income tax.
"Germany wants to get her industry motoring again," he said, adding that the move could leave France lagging behind and thus have serious consequences for the EMU convergence process.
Analysts said Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan could of course surprise markets with a rise.
"I understand there is a general consensus that rates aren't going to go up, and if I were Alan Greenspan, I might think that was a good reason to do it," said Smith.
